title: Kush: the African kingdom that ruled Egypt
subtitle: In the eighth century BCE, rulers from what is now Sudan became pharaohs of Egypt.

parts.text: Ancient Egypt is usually told as a story on its own. Its southern neighbour, Kush, was a power in its own right, and for a time ruled Egypt.
Kush occupied the region of modern Sudan, later called Nubia.
The Kerma culture was one of the great empires of the second millennium BCE.

parts.text: The Kerma museum site gives Napatan from about 730 BCE and Meroitic from about 400 BCE; the University of Chicago says the capital moved to Meroe in the third century BCE.
This page gives each date as its source states it and does not try to draw one neat line between periods.

items.text: Early, Middle and Classic Kerma, as the Kerma museum divides it.
Piankhy, king of Napata, undertakes the pacification of Egypt and establishes the Twenty-Fifth Dynasty, on the Kerma museum's account.
Taharqa has already lost control of Lower Egypt to Ashurbanipal.
Tanutamani is defeated again by the Assyrians.
The capital of the Napatan empire moves south to Meroe.
Ezana, king of the Aksumite Empire, invades and occupies Meroe.

blocks.prompt: In which year BCE does National Geographic say Taharqa had already lost Lower Egypt to the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal?

parts.text: 667 BCE; Tanutamani was defeated again in 663 BCE.
Kashta took over Upper Egypt, followed by his son Piankhi, who controlled all of Egypt in what became known as the Twenty-Fifth Dynasty.
The Kerma museum likewise credits Piankhy with establishing the dynasty.
Taharqa had already lost control of Lower Egypt to Ashurbanipal in 667 BCE, and Tanutamani was defeated again in 663 BCE.
Some popular accounts credit Kashta alone with founding the Twenty-Fifth Dynasty. The sources read here give Piankhi, his son, the role of ruling all of Egypt.

image.caption: The pyramids at Meroë, Sudan.

parts.text: The capital of the Napatan empire moved south to Meroe in the third century BCE.
Meroe has extensive slagheaps from iron working.
One study of its charcoal says the data point neither to fuel shortage nor to environmental degradation, which questions the older idea that iron smelting stripped the land of trees.
A 1983 article by the archaeologist Krzysztof Grzymski says that the Meroitic scripts can be read, but the language they are written in is still unknown.

blocks.q: What does Grzymski say about the Meroitic script?
options: It can be read, but the language is still unknown
Both script and language are fully understood
It is the same as Egyptian hieroglyphs
blocks.answer: It can be read, but the language is still unknown
blocks.explain: In 'The Meroitic Mystery' (1983), Grzymski writes that the Meroitic scripts can be read, but the language they are written in is still unknown.

gaps: Left out because the readable sources contradict or do not support it: Kashta as founder of the dynasty, the date of 590 BCE for the sack of Napata, deforestation caused by iron working, and the fall of the kingdom about 350 CE.
The Metropolitan Museum pages on Kush could not be opened (error 429) and are not cited; they are the likeliest source for the periods and for King Arkamani I.
Periods and dates differ between sources; the Kerma museum and the University of Chicago give different boundaries and this page reports each.
The Meroitic article is from 1983 and may be out of date on how much of the language is understood.
The Carey study was read only in abstract; Török's The Kingdom of Kush or Edwards's The Nubian Past should be read next.

keyPoints.text: Kush occupied the region of modern Sudan, later called Nubia, and Kerma was one of the great empires of the second millennium BCE.
Kashta took over Upper Egypt, followed by his son Piankhi, who controlled all of Egypt in what became the Twenty-Fifth Dynasty.
National Geographic dates the Assyrian defeats of Taharqa and Tanutamani to 667 and 663 BCE.
The Meroitic scripts can be read, but the language they write is still unknown.
